🎉 Congrats to @Zai_org on GLM-5.3-Flash, the first natively multimodal model in the GLM-5 series, and their first hybrid of sparse and linear attention.

320B total, 18B active, 45 layers where GLM-4.5 had 92. Linear attention carries local dependencies as state, sparse attention pulls global context back through a lightweight indexer, and IndexPool weights four indexer key vectors into one to keep that indexer cheap at 1M tokens. mHC on top, for scaling.

vLLM already had each half of that mix. This is the first model to ask for both at once, and it has day-0 support, verified on @NVIDIA and @AMD GPUs.

MiniMax H3 Max, a post-trained version of MiniMax H3 developed by fal, debuts at #1 in Image to Video and #3 in Text to Video on the Artificial Analysis Video Leaderboards with Audio, ahead of the base MiniMax H3 on both

MiniMax H3 Max is built and served by fal, and post-trained from MiniMax H3. fal describes it as being tuned for stronger prompt adherence and better aesthetics, co-optimized with their custom inference stack for higher throughput. It generates 5 to 15 second clips with native audio at up to 768p.

In the Artificial Analysis Video Arena, H3 Max ranks #1 in Image to Video with Audio, narrowly ahead of ByteDance's Dreamina Seedance 2.0 720p. It ranks #3 in Text to Video with Audio, on a board where the top three models sit within 6 points of each other.

fal prices MiniMax H3 Max at $0.04 per second of 768p video ($2.40 per minute). The base MiniMax H3 endpoint on fal is $0.06 per second at the same resolution.

fal has stated its intent to release the weights for MiniMax H3 Max. If it does, H3 Max would become the highest ranked open weights model on both boards, ahead of MiniMax H3, which leads on open weights today.

Congratulations to @fal on the release!

items.title: We benchmarked 20+ open-weight models on easy-to-hard document extraction tasks through ExtractBench...
items.content:
We benchmarked 20+ open-weight models on easy-to-hard document extraction tasks through ExtractBench. The results are all available on @huggingface 🤗

ExtractBench is a schema-guided extraction benchmark that contains 4.8k+ pages across 8 domains and 67 document types, with a mix of short, medium, long docs and simple/complex schema.s

The results reported is a measure of “value accuracy” through unified F1.
✅ Qwen 3.8 leads the pack
✅ earlier generations of Qwen models are also quite strong
✅ kimi-k3 is the next best.

GLM-5.3-flash and qwen 3.8 flash also just released today - hopefully will have results on these soon!

Note : these results don’t include visual grounding (whether each value is mapped to the right bounding box) and confidence scores. When you include these, it is increasingly clear why specialized OCR tools (like LlamaParse) matter, since this is metadata that’s hard to DIY by prompting the raw model.

Come check out our HF leaderboard: https://t.co/WHW5A6n5LU

Learn more about ExtractBench here: https://t.co/VapjcfLa1B

items.title: Google has released Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, ranking #5 on AA-WER at 2.6%, alongside Gemini 3.5 Transc...
items.content:
Google has released Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, ranking #5 on AA-WER at 2.6%, alongside Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live, achieving 4.0% AA-WER Streaming at 0.40s after speech end

@GoogleAI's Gemini 3.5 Transcribe release comprises two API offerings: Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live for continuous streaming through the Live API, and Gemini 3.5 Transcribe for pre-recorded audio through the Interactions API. Both support 85+ languages, custom vocabulary and automatic text formatting, while the pre-recorded API adds timestamped multi-speaker identification for up to three speakers, with support beyond three currently experimental.

Key takeaways
➤ Non-streaming transcription: Gemini 3.5 Transcribe achieves 2.6% AA-WER, ranking #5 overall, and processes audio at approximately 84× realtime.

items.title: The issue I have with computer-use models today is that they spend too much time clicking through in...
items.content:
The issue I have with computer-use models today is that they spend too much time clicking through interfaces.

You can die of boredom waiting for these tools to finish a simple task.

n2 is a new 27B-parameter computer-use model that handles this differently.

When solving a problem, the model chooses how to complete each step based on the fastest available option.

The model works in 4 different ways:

1. Use a GUI to interact with an application
2. Write terminal commands to work with the operating system
3. Call an API to access a service directly
4. Write code to handle a task programmatically

As n2 works through a task, it switches between these options, and the end result is a much faster solution!

For example, to complete a specific workflow, the model may browse the web, open an application, edit one file, run a few commands, and call an API.

This is key when you are building agents that work across different tools. You want these agents to be faster, less fragile, and be able to work for longer.

You can test the API and interactive playground at https://t.co/G1x2wLqo3R.

Thanks to the Yutori team for partnering with me on this post.

And we cover how physical understanding doesn't just help with replacing experiments but lets us optimize design directly.

items.title: Reinforcement learning—where a program learns by acting in an environment and observing rewards—has ...
items.content:
Reinforcement learning—where a program learns by acting in an environment and observing rewards—has an unusually fragile experimental setup: two implementations of the same idea can look quite different because of random initialization, the data encountered during learning, hyperparameter choices, evaluation length, or seemingly minor environment details, so a clean-looking performance graph can support a much stronger claim than the experiment really justifies.

Patterson and colleagues from @AmiiThinks and @UAlberta organize these problems into a practical account of how to design experiments that separate real algorithmic differences from noise and researcher choices: they explain how to measure variation across runs, distinguish uncertainty about an average from variation among individual agents, choose enough runs, handle hyperparameters without giving one method an unfair advantage, compare algorithms more carefully, and select environments that reveal specific strengths or failures rather than merely produce rankings.

They also introduce several concrete methods for making comparisons more reliable and finish with a detailed re-analysis of Soft Actor-Critic and DDPG showing that additional runs, implementation details, and better tuning of the baseline can substantially change the apparent conclusion of a well-known experiment.

- Four reps and 10,000 inbound leads a da...
items.content:
What engineering go to market looks like, from ten teams:

- Four reps and 10,000 inbound leads a day. Nine months later, when the enterprise product finally shipped, prospects said "you never got back to me." Automate the reply before you hire the team
- A cookie banner library's number one source of inbound since April is coding agents recommending it. Coding agents never read the website for a library, they read node_modules, so the docs now ship inside the package
- An internal GTM assistant has answered a million questions for 6,000 sellers. Two weeks after launch, one in five had tried it. The rule: 50 questions at 95% beats 100 at 70%
- Ask an assistant to compare code intelligence tools and Sourcegraph comes up 65% of the time. Describe the pain it solves instead: zero mentions
- Cloudflare's weekly GTM summary is written by three agents: one drafts from the data, one checks the draft against the data, one fixes the tone. The team read every run for two to three months first

https://t.co/9NoHNybmmh

items.title: GLM-5.3-Flash scores 57 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. At $0.09 Cost per Task, it si...
items.content:
GLM-5.3-Flash scores 57 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. At $0.09 Cost per Task, it sits comfortably on the Intelligence vs. Cost per Task Pareto frontier

@Zai_org has released GLM-5.3-Flash, a smaller and cheaper sibling to GLM-5.3 at 320B total parameters and just 18B active parameters. GLM-5.3-Flash supports low/high/max reasoning efforts, and scores 57 evaluation on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with max reasoning effort. This places the model only 3 points behind GLM-5.3 at 60 and in line with GPT-5.6 Terra and Muse Spark 1.2.

On Z AI's first-party API, GLM-5.3-Flash is priced at $0.15 / 1M input tokens and $0.50 / 1M output tokens, just over 10% of the price of GLM-5.3. Cached input tokens are priced at $0.026 / 1M tokens, an 80% discount. Its Cost per Task on the Intelligence Index is $0.09, compared to $0.68 for GLM-5.3 (max), and it sits on the Pareto frontier for Intelligence vs. Cost per Task.

Key results:

➤ GLM-5.3-Flash is 3 points behind GLM-5.3 (max) on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, at ~7.5x lower Cost per Task. At $0.09 per Intelligence Index task against $0.68 for GLM-5.3, it sits on the Pareto frontier for Intelligence vs. Cost per Task. It ties GPT-5.6 Terra ($0.51) and Muse Spark 1.2 ($0.40) at 57 while costing ~5.7x and ~4.4x less per task.

➤ GLM-5.3-Flash is less token efficient, but its low per-token pricing means this does not translate into a high Cost per Task. The model used 149M output tokens to run the Intelligence Index, ~11% fewer than GLM-5.3 at 168M, but more than Kimi K3 (133M) and Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B (136M) which score the same on the Intelligence Index. Reasoning tokens account for 134M of the 149M total (~90%).

➤ GLM-5.3-Flash matches GLM-5.3 on real-world agentic work on GDPval-AA v2. With an Elo of 1770, the model is tied within the margin of error for GLM-5.3 and Grok 4.6. LLM Buffer: Ordered Request, FCFS Scheduling, Queue Blocking, Buffer Result Queu, and Ordered Output - by - @thisisUIC - University of Illinois Chicago

In LLM serving, requests can enter an ordered queue buffer: 
 
R0 
R1 
R2 
R3 

Under chronological First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) scheduling, a long request at the front can delay shorter requests behind it classic line blocking.

These concepts appear elsewhere across AI systems. PyTorch DataLoader can leverage multiple workers that finish batches asynchronously, while in_order=True preserves FIFO delivery by holding out-of-order results until the expected batch buffer can be returned conceptually Result Buffer Queue, Reorder/Holding Buffer, Ordered Output.

In Reinforcement Learning, replay buffers store experience tuples over time. 

LLM inference engines similarly leverage request buffer queues and scheduling policies to manage work before GPU execution.

UIC researchers visualize FCFS scheduling in From Prompts to Priorities: Pairwise Learning-to-Rank Scheduling for Low-Latency LLM Serving Buffer.

Hosting the 2nd founder dinner in sf on August 31 with @GuangyuRobert at @Fundamental - the team behind @tryshortcutai

Agents are increasingly capable of solving tasks for longer task horizons without human in the loop. This has rewarded "horizontal" products owned by the frontier lab, like Codex and Claude Code, which let users specify a broad range of tasks through a single interface.  

For startups to survive, is the moat around: 
- Product (can you build a differentiated interface from Cowork) 
- Harness (can you build a more differentiated agent for a given set of tasks) 
- Data (can you accumulate a proprietary set of data that frontier models are not trained on) 
- Deep domain and workflow expertise (can you learn more about a business than OpenAI can) 
- Brand / mindshare (you're more well known for a particular thing than a frontier model) 

RSVP here: https://t.co/0dmtxySEEi

Really interesting new blog post from @openai for several reasons:

1) Shows an example of building with WebMCP,  meant for when you want agents and and humans to collaborate on using a UI (like co-editing notebook cells).   It's different than MCPs or APIs in that its exposed directly through the browser.  Read the post for discussion of the tradeoffs.

2) They created a new kind of notebook which works with WebMCP  that prioritizes meeting people where they are:  you bring your own coding agent and files are just markdown.  The author uses it to curate runbooks or high quality examples of how to run foundation model evals on their infrastructure.  Notebooks are good for this since they require tinkering with state of long running jobs interactively while taking notes inline.  And its open source ✨

Blog: https://t.co/tW8zpbkZNp

P.S. this post is authored by Jeremy Lewi who isn't on X but here is his website https://t.co/hhdEV8t7jc
